Eight hours is how long the evacuation reportedly took. Tim Kennedy, a Green Beret and former UFC fighter, was hit three times in the leg on September 17, in an ambush in South Kivu that killed at least seven Congolese and a New Zealand SAS veteran, Justin Conaglen, who had left the military only weeks earlier. A third operator was wounded. Kennedy is now at Walter Reed in stable condition, and New Zealand has opened its own investigation into Conaglen's death.

The mission is worth reading twice. Eastern Congo holds cobalt, copper and gold, the raw material of every phone and electric car battery, and the region has been at war over it for decades. M23, which the UN says Rwanda backs, took Goma and Bukavu last year. Congo's answer was to hire help. Vectus Global, a firm linked to Blackwater founder Erik Prince, was brought in to protect mining revenue, and its work has since drifted toward military operations. Reuters reports this was its first casualty event in the country.

Who fired is the part still unsettled. Three Reuters sources say the ambush was too sophisticated for anyone but Rwandan forces, and one says the attackers may have followed a surveillance drone to the team's location. A competing rumor names Russia's Africa Corps, the successor to Wagner. No one has produced proof of that, and the reporting points the other way.

The detail I keep returning to is smaller. As of last year, Kennedy was a part-time master sergeant in the Maryland National Guard. If that has not changed, a serving American soldier was shot while working private security for a foreign government. Guard members can hold civilian jobs, so the question is not whether that is allowed in principle. It is whether anyone in uniform knew, and whether anyone approved it.

Someone signed off, or no one did. Either answer is the story.

All of it is reportedly sourced to anonymous officials, and Kennedy, Vectus and the Pentagon have not commented.
